one_liner: Header-only C++20 io_uring (SQPOLL, fixed files and buffers) O_DIRECT block I/O engine; out-runs Boost.Asio file I/O and Go on 4 KiB writes.
what_it_does: FluxIO is a Linux block-I/O engine for 4 KiB-page O_DIRECT reads, writes and fdatasync on a small set of registered files. You push flux::IORequest structs into an SPSC submission ring, call process_submissions(), then poll_completion() and try_pop_completion() for flux::IoCompletion records; it is not a drop-in for pread/pwrite, iostreams or Asio. flux::flux_storage_engine picks the io_uring backend when liburing.h is present and a synchronous pread/pwrite O_DIRECT backend otherwise, and pybind11 bindings are included.
how_it_is_fast: It sets up io_uring with IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL so a kernel thread polls the submission queue (no io_uring_enter per batch while it is awake), registers the file descriptors (IOSQE_FIXED_FILE) and a pool of page-aligned buffers (io_uring_register_buffers, read_fixed/write_fixed) so the kernel skips per-I/O fd lookup and page pinning. Free buffer slots come from a 128-bit bitmask allocated with ctz, and request/completion queues are cache-line-aligned SPSC rings. FileBlockManager fallocate()s 10 MB chunks with FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE ahead of the write frontier (80% watermark) to cut extent allocation on sparse files.
when_to_use: Linux NVMe workloads issuing many independent 4 KiB O_DIRECT reads or writes at queue depth 4-128 from one thread, e.g. a storage engine, log or block cache.
When you can spare a second core for the SQPOLL kernel thread in exchange for higher IOPS from a single submitting thread.
Write-heavy streams into preallocated files, where it measured about 0.5-0.7 M IOPS (sequential and random 4 KiB writes) on a consumer NVMe drive.
As a compact, readable example of SQPOLL plus fixed files and buffers to copy into your own engine (MIT, a few headers).
when_not_to_use: Sequential reads: it measured 278,054.8 IOPS vs Go's 302,860.5 (0.92x), and IOPS per core is roughly on par with Go once the SQPOLL thread is counted (README).
Requests larger than the page size (default 4096 B): each request must fit one registered buffer, so larger I/O must be split by the caller.
Non-Linux, buffered or non-x86 environments: io_uring and O_DIRECT only, and the code calls __builtin_ia32_rdtsc directly for timestamps.
Multi-threaded submission: rings are single-producer/single-consumer and the engine holds no locks.
Production use without your own testing: 9 commits in under a week (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-04), no CVE or issue history, and the benchmark harness does not check per-I/O results.

integration.dependencies: liburing (optional; without it the POSIX pread/pwrite backend is used), pthread; pybind11 only for the Python module
integration.platforms: Linux only; io_uring backend effectively x86-64 (direct __builtin_ia32_rdtsc and pause calls); SQPOLL may need root or CAP_SYS_NICE on older kernels (README runs the benchmark with sudo)
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded per engine: lock-free SPSC submission and completion rings, one producer and one consumer

gotchas: The README headline 'QD128 random write with FileBlockManager 429,229.3 IOPS vs Go 29,074.7 and Asio 28,411.3' uses FluxIO's QD16 row: its own Mode 2 table shows 28,335.9 IOPS at QD128 (and 16,816.5 at QD64), the same as the Go and Asio sparse-file numbers, so the claimed fix for the ext4 inode-lock collapse is not supported at QD128.

bench_fluxio.cpp counts every completion as a finished op and never checks comp.failed or comp.result, so failed or short I/Os would still inflate IOPS; register_file silently reopens without O_DIRECT if the filesystem returns EINVAL, which would turn the run into page-cache I/O.

io_uring register_file() only opens files that already exist (it never passes O_CREAT on a missing path) and a failed open hits FLUXIO_SAFE_CHECK, which calls abort(); the POSIX backend does create the file.

Writes are memcpy'd into the registered buffer and reads are copied out of it on completion, so 'fixed buffers' does not mean zero-copy for the caller; the SQPOLL thread spins for 2000 ms after each burst (sq_thread_idle).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over raw liburing when you want SQPOLL, fixed files and buffers, slot management and fallocate-ahead already wired up for 4 KiB O_DIRECT blocks; pick liburing itself (or SPDK for full userspace NVMe) when you need arbitrary request sizes, multiple threads, or measured, mature behavior.
verified_claims_summary: First-party runs of benchmark/bench_fluxio.cpp (4 KiB O_DIRECT, 20,000-50,000 ops per point, QD 1-128, 256 MB file, thread pinned to core 2, consumer NVMe, CPU model not stated) peak at 715,827.6 IOPS sequential and 542,998.1 random write vs Go os.O_DIRECT with goroutines (239,383.5 and 248,800.8) and Boost.Asio C++20 file I/O (86,783.1 and 86,821.4), using about 200% CPU vs about 100%. The Go and Asio harnesses are not in the repo, and the sparse-file QD128 comparison quotes FluxIO's QD16 result.
status_note: Active but brand new (9 commits, 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-04, 6 stars, no issues); MIT and small enough to vendor, but treat it as a reference design rather than a hardened dependency.
